children.translated_text: <s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight)

body.translated_text: Composed by the illustrious poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, [author of] <s>Pīyūṣavarṣa</s> (Shower of Nectar)

children.translated_text: She who causes the lotus-quality to droop exceedingly, who by her manifest spots

children.text: dhvaṃsaṃ hastayate ca yā sumanasām ullāsinī mānase
children.translated_text: destroys and handles the lotuses, who delights in the minds of the good,
Bold, with rising fire that destroyed <s>Madana</s>, pure, showing the three worlds --
May that <s>Vāgdevatā</s> (Goddess of Speech), like the three eyes of the axe-wielding <s>Khaṇḍaparaśu</s> (Śiva), shine forth!
Ho! O <s>cintāmaṇi</s>-gems of the consciousness-mind-moon, nourish the <s>rasas</s> (aesthetic sentiments)!

children.text: re re svairiṇi nirvicārakavite māsmat prakāśībhava
children.translated_text: O wayward poet devoid of discrimination, do not shine forth from us!
For the delight of the ocean of ornaments consisting of waves of contemplation,
<s>Pīyūṣavarṣa</s> (Shower of Nectar), the skilled one, himself spreads the <s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight).
The sole abode of brilliant <s>rasas</s> to be savored through skill, the literary <s>Sārasvata</s>
milk-ocean, assuming unfathomable depth -- let it be resorted to and embraced;
From this [comes] <s>Śrī</s> (prosperity); from this, nectar consisting of skill in instruction; from this, the world
awakens -- O wise ones, [resort to this] moon of the fame of the lotus-sun <s>Padmakeśara</s>!
We praise that [master] from whom arose a host of luminaries
from the sun-utterances of former <s>ācāryas</s> (teachers);
Having introduced whom,
my qualities shine forth like motes in a sunbeam.
It should not be doubted that their
doctrine is criticized by this [work];
Rather, the eyes of the doe-eyed women
are adorned as if by collyrium.
<s>Pratibhā</s> (creative intuition) alone, accompanied by
learning and practice, is the cause of poetry --
Like a garland of seeds bound with clay and water
[is the cause] of a creeping vine.
Speech that is free from faults, possessing characteristics,
having beautiful composition, adorned with <s>guṇas</s> (qualities),
endowed with <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments) and various <s>rasas</s> (sentiments),
and having [appropriate] <s>vṛtti</s> (style) -- bears the name of <s>kāvya</s> (poetry).
He who accepts that <s>kāvya</s> (poetry) consists of
<s>śabda</s> (word) and <s>artha</s> (meaning) without ornamentation --
why does that wise one not consider
a fire without heat to be [still] a fire?
A word capable of generating case-endings
is considered a grammatical word (<s>śāstrīya śabda</s>);
It is again threefold through the divisions of
<s>rūḍhi</s> (conventional), <s>yaugika</s> (etymological), and <s>miśra</s> (mixed).
The first (<s>rūḍhi</s>) is threefold: with obscure connection (<s>avyaktayoga</s>),
without connection (<s>niryoga</s>), and with semblance of connection (<s>yogābhāsa</s>);
These are respectively [exemplified by] 'tree' etc., 'earth' etc.,
and 'pavilion' etc.
The etymological (<s>yaugika</s>) is threefold: pure, root-derived,
and compound-derived;
These respectively take the form of '<s>bhrānti</s>' (error), '<s>sphurat</s>' (shining), '<s>kānti</s>' (beauty),
and '<s>Kaunteya</s>' (son of Kuntī) etc.
The mixed (<s>miśra</s>) [arises] from the interchange
of the general and particular of each other;
[Examples:] '<s>nīradhi</s>' (ocean), '<s>paṅkaja</s>' (lotus), '<s>saudha</s>' (palace),
'<s>sāgara</s>' (ocean), '<s>bhūruha</s>' (tree), '<s>śaśin</s>' (moon).
'<s>Kṣīranīradhi</s>' (milk-ocean) [and] 'sky-
lotus' -- thereby [the mixed type] is established.
A word ending in a case-suffix is a <s>pada</s> (word-unit); a <s>vākya</s> (sentence)
is their arrangement, from the completion of meaning.
Without that connected meaning,
it is considered a <s>khaṇḍavākya</s> (incomplete sentence);
Both a sentence and an incomplete sentence
can sometimes consist of even a single word.
'Because of having smoke' -- thus [is a single-word sentence];
'O God!' -- thus [is an example of] a vocative [sentence].
Sentences resting in a single meaning
are called a <s>vākyakadambaka</s> (cluster of sentences).
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in the lore of sacrifices led by <s>Satra</s>,
<s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted through devotion to him -- these two were his parents.
By this [chapter], may that first <s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray), in the <s>Candrāloka</s> composed by the good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>,
long delight the good-hearted ones!
That by which entering the mind,
the perceived charm [is destroyed] --
manifesting in word and meaning,
they proclaim that a <s>doṣa</s> (fault).
A sound that is harsh to the ear,
adept at causing displeasure to hearing --
[is called] <s>śrutikaṭu</s> (ear-grating). [A word] opposed to grammar
[is called] <s>cyutasaṃskṛti</s> (fallen from correct form).
<s>Aprayukta</s> (unused) is [a word] like '<s>daivatā</s>' etc. --
using masculine gender etc. for words [that are otherwise];
<s>Asamartha</s> (incapable) is the use of '<s>hanti</s>' (kills) etc.
in the sense of 'going' etc.
'He kills (hanti), alas (hanta)! in the wilderness,
the beloved one with curling locks.'
<s>Nihatārtha</s> (debased meaning) is the use of '<s>śoṇita</s>' (blood) etc.
in place of '<s>lohita</s>' (red) etc.
That which reveals an inappropriate meaning --
they call that word itself [the fault called] <s>anucitārtha</s> (unfitting meaning).
'This [woman], on the foremost branch of a wonderful tree,
is a monkey of amorous sport and curiosity.'
<s>Nirarthaka</s> (meaningless) is '<s>tu</s>', '<s>hi</s>' etc.,
whose sole purpose is padding;
<s>Avācaka</s> (non-expressive) is like 'vidadhat' etc.,
conferring [incorrect form like] 'dadhat' etc. on the meaning.
'The sun holds the sky
ruddy with youthful rays.'
<s>Ekākṣara</s> (monosyllabic [fault]) is [using] 'bhū', 'bhrū',
'kṣmā' etc., like 'kha', 'ta', 'la' etc.
<s>Aślīla</s> (obscene) is threefold: through shame,
disgust, and inauspiciousness.
'How can wind be the cause of delight
when the beloved is lost?'
<s>Sandigdha</s> (ambiguous) would be a [word with] double meaning here:
'Birds go in the river.'
<s>Apratīta</s> (obscure) would be [a meaning] knowable
only through scripture, like '<s>vītānuma</s>' etc.
<s>Śithila</s> (loose) -- 'On the bed I dissolved,
my mind [fixed] on your moon-beauty.'
'<s>Masta</s>', '<s>piṣṭaka</s>', '<s>kaṭī</s>', '<s>loṣṭa</s>',
'<s>galla</s>' etc. are called <s>grāmya</s> (vulgar).
<s>Neyārtha</s> (requiring interpretation) -- due to excessive extension
of <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary meaning), it becomes unpleasing.
'The rays of the moon that put necklaces to shame
keep awake the night-watchmen.'
<s>Kliṣṭa</s> (forced) -- when its meaning ascends
a stairless series of meanings.
'Words like the stream of the daughter-in-law
of the father of <s>Hari</s>'s beloved.'
<s>Avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa</s> (unconsidered predicate) -- when the predicate
is concealed by a compound:
'The sidelong glances of beautiful women, like arrows,
enter the heart with a smile.'
'<s>Aparādhīna</s>' etc. --
[is the fault] <s>viruddhamati</s> (contradictory understanding) that produces a contrary notion.
<s>Anyasaṅgata</s> (misconnected) -- 'Her breasts that are beautiful
with lofty necklaces.'
When a sound is inappropriate for the <s>rasa</s> (sentiment) etc.,
the learned call it <s>pratikūlākṣara</s> (hostile syllable).
'Do you not know me, <s>Aṅgada</s>?
I am <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, terrible in battle!'
Where the <s>visarga</s> is damaged or lost,
that is [the fault called] thus.
<s>Kusandhi</s> (bad junction) -- '<s>paṭav āgaccha</s>';
<s>Visandhi</s> (disjunction) -- '<s>nṛpatī imau</s>'.
<s>Hatavṛtta</s> (destroyed meter) -- even when unstated,
the metrical fault is apparent:
'O wide-eyed one! Behold
the sky undulating with stars!'
<s>Nyūna</s> (deficient) -- 'The firmament [is not large enough for] the fame-flowers
born of your sword.'
<s>Adhika</s> (excessive) -- 'Your sword-creeper's hood
bites your enemies.'
<s>Punarukta</s> (tautology) is speech that states the already stated --
'the dark-lotus-dark-eyed one.'
<s>Vikṛta</s> (distorted) is [produced] by widely separated [vowels] --
'<s>aiyaruḥ kuñjarāḥ puram</s>'.
<s>Patatprakarṣa</s> (falling eminence) -- when there is descending order of excellence
instead of ascending, as in:
'This one whose hand [wields] a thunderbolt, of deep enterprise,
has arrived!'
<s>Samāptapunarātta</s> (completed-then-resumed) would be:
'This is a vessel of nectar --
the moon that delights the eyes
rises, kinsman of the ocean.'
<s>Ardhāntarapadāpekṣin</s> (expecting an intervening word) --
'In sport and dance, with a smile,
we praise <s>Śambhu</s> of fruitless endeavor,
whose body is half that of <s>Rambhā</s> (the golden-thighed one).'
<s>Abhavanmatayoga</s> (impossible construal) -- when
the intended syntactic connection does not exist:
'By whom the ocean was bound, whose
we are the servants of <s>Rāma</s>.'
'Having seized the prosperity of enemies,
who filled the foes [with grief]' --
<s>Asthānasthasamāsa</s> (compound in wrong place) -- not
pleasing to the minds of the learned.
<s>Saṃkīrṇa</s> (confused) is when separate sentence-words
are mutually [entangled] -- that itself [is the fault]:
'The night shines with [her] face;
the beloved shines with the moon.'
'The universe, O ornament of the earth, is filled
with the flood of your fame;
Listen -- [it appears like] a golden jar
full of water.'
<s>Bhagnaprakrama</s> (broken sequence) -- inability to complete
the word that was begun:
<s>Akrama</s> (disorder) -- 'O <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>! Deities are worshipped
without worshipping you.'
<s>Amatārthāntara</s> (unintended secondary meaning) -- when a non-primary meaning
creates contradiction with the primary meaning:
'Having abandoned the necklace on her chest,
the woman was embraced by grief.'
<s>Apuṣṭārtha</s> (unsupported meaning) -- when the qualifier
does not distinguish the qualified:
'The sidelong glances of the beloved,
having the lustre of a wagtail bird, enter the heart.'
<s>Kaṣṭa</s> (difficult) -- incapable of conveying clear understanding,
resembling the stated [meaning but obscure].
<s>Vyāhata</s> (contradicted) -- when there is contradiction
between the earlier and later meanings.
'Your face, O friend of the thousand-petaled [lotus] --
to what can it be compared?'
'From where is there a simile, when
even the moon would be a repetition?'
These three faults -- <s>duṣkrama</s> (bad sequence), <s>grāmya</s> (vulgar),
and <s>sandigdha</s> (ambiguous) -- are respectively [illustrated]:
'O <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>! Being your devotee, I would go
to hell or even to heaven.'
'Give me one kiss;
I shall give you a bodice.'
'Tell me -- which of the two should be served:
the moon-faced one or the moon-crested one?'
<s>Anaucitya</s> (impropriety) -- that which always
causes the vine of fame to waver.
Through common usage or through learning,
the contradicted [type] is considered twofold.
'Behold! This [ketakī], with the white radiance
of <s>Kandarpa</s>'s (Love's) prowess,
the <s>ketakī</s> flower on <s>Śambhu</s>'s crest
bears resemblance to the crescent moon.'
<s>Sāmānyaparivṛtti</s> (violation of the general) would be:
'[She] with a body [beautiful as] the lustre of earrings.'
<s>Viśeṣaparivṛtti</s> (violation of the particular) would be:
'The woman [rests] in my mind.'
Likewise, the beautiful association
of mutually contradictory [things]:
'Crows and saints do not know
their own and another's son.'
'O lotus-eyed one! Behold the moon-face
of your son!
He shall protect your lineage --
he is an <s>Indra</s> among men!'
In a word, in a part of a word, in a part of a sentence,
in a sentence, in a cluster of sentences --
one should infer faults
arising from word and meaning as appropriate.
That which restrains a fault that has arisen in the mind,
spreading unbridled --
they call it a <s>doṣāṅkuśa</s> (goad against faults),
which is threefold.
It either converts the fault into a <s>guṇa</s> (quality),
or removes the fault-nature,
or else renders the fault
unavoidable [and thus acceptable].
'The face bears the beauty of the moon
with the white sprouts of beard and hands.'
Here, in the context of <s>hāsyarasa</s> (comic sentiment),
vulgarity has attained the status of a <s>guṇa</s> (quality).
'O you who are born of the milk-ocean,
how have you become spotted?'
Through the convention of poets, the learned
[say this] contradicted [meaning] has attained the status of non-fault.
'<s>Gaurī</s> (Pārvatī) held in her heart
the lord marked with the moon.'
Here, due to the arising of <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning), the meaningless '<s>hi</s>'
is indeed not to be rejected.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in the lore of sacrifices led by <s>Satra</s>,
<s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted through devotion to him -- these two were his parents.
By that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed [work], may this second
<s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray) of the <s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight) long delight the good-hearted!
<s>Śobhā</s> (lustre) is a grouping of syllables
consisting of few letters and varied meanings.
'Followed by <s>Uṣā</s>'s husband (<s>Aniruddha</s>),
this hero <s>Śauri</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) [appears] again!'
<s>Śobhā</s> -- even when a well-known [word's] fault
is negated by praising its quality:
'In vain they censure <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence),
where the enemy of <s>Kaṃsa</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) is worshipped!'
<s>Abhimāna</s> (pride/attribution) -- if it is a deliberation that
negates a conceived meaning:
'If it is the moon, why is it fierce?
If it is the sun, why at night?'
<s>Hetu</s> (reasoning) -- abandoning many alternatives,
the ascertainment of one through logic:
'It is not the moon, not the sun -- this is the submarine fire (<s>aurvāgni</s>),
risen from the ocean, burning!'
<s>Pratiṣedha</s> (denial) -- the disregard
of well-known causes:
'Not by battle, but by the motion of her brows
alone were the heroes felled.'
<s>Nirukta</s> (etymology) would be an etymological explanation
of a name, either true or false:
'O King, with such deeds as these,
you are truly a "maker of faults" (doṣā-kara = moon)!'
<s>Mithyādhyavasāya</s> (false determination) -- when
both the means and end are unreal:
'Wear a garland of sky-flowers
strung on threads of moonbeams!'
<s>Siddhi</s> (establishment) -- when among famous [things],
a name is mentioned to state equality:
'You two alone are renowned here --
you by your powers, and the ocean by its waters.'
<s>Yukti</s> (reasoning) -- the establishment of a particular
through connection with varied other meanings:
'You are some extraordinary rain-cloud,
since you rain gold repeatedly!'
<s>Kārya</s> (effect) -- the apprehension of a result
from an action or from a thing:
'The cool-rayed moon rises
to destroy the pride of beautiful women.'
Thus and more -- the great sages declare
numerous characteristics of <s>kāvya</s> (poetry),
as [many attributes are declared] of kings, such as
having a forehead brilliant as gold.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in the lore of sacrifices led by <s>Satra</s>,
<s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted through devotion to him -- these two were his parents.
By that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed [work], may this third
<s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray) of the <s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight) long delight the good-hearted!
<s>Śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) is the description of a meaning dissolving
[while another] forms simultaneously.
The verbal [type] is a binding with words of the same class,
producing delight.
When the slenderness [of her body] was brought to full manifestation
by the thorns of horripilation at the end [of the embrace],
[it was as if] by the frightened <s>Mānavatī</s> (proud lady) herself --
we praise <s>Hari</s> embraced by <s>Śrī</s> (Lakṣmī)!
Since all meaning within [the word]
shines forth by itself --
like [the clarity] of water -- that [quality] of well-spoken speech
is called <s>prasāda</s> (clarity/grace).
<s>Samatā</s> (evenness) is having few compounds,
or equality in syllables etc.:
'The dark, tender maiden
has gone to her lover as refuge.'
<s>Samādhi</s> (concentration) is the grandeur of meaning
with the nature of dense, brilliant <s>rasa</s>;
By which, entering within,
the limbs of the good are made to bristle.
<s>Mādhurya</s> (sweetness) is [when] repetition
produces charm through variety:
'O friend, look, look at the restless
corner of her eyes!'
<s>Ojas</s> (vigor) is the boldness of meaning,
or compression of the excessive:
'Having slain the enemy, having earned fame,
your sword entered the scabbard.'
<s>Saukumārya</s> (delicacy) is the absence of harshness
through the turning of synonyms:
'He has become a mere tale,
having embraced the friend of the wind (<s>Agni</s>, fire).'
<s>Udāratā</s> (nobility) is elegance,
distinctiveness from non-vulgarity:
'Abandon your pride, O beloved! Raise
a little the corner of your eye.'
In <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) and in clarity,
<s>kānti</s> (charm) is the grasp of explicit meaning.
These ten <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) in <s>kāvya</s> (poetry)
are like valor etc. in a man.
Like the <s>tilaka</s>-mark and other ornaments of women,
Reaching the heart of the connoisseur,
<s>Alaṅkāra</s> (poetic figure), distinct [from the natural quality of speech],
Is the ornament of speech, [adorning] its nature.
Varied definitions, establishment,
Completion, maturity, propriety,
Expression of the secrets of other <s>śāstras</s>,
Compilation — the direction has been shown.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, singularly skilled in the knowledge of <s>sattra</s>-led sacrifices,
And <s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted in devotion to him — these being his parents,
May this fourth [ray], in the <s>Candrāloka</s> composed by the good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>,
Long delight the good-hearted with its radiance.
Through the renown of word and meaning,
Or through the poet's mastery,
<s>Alaṅkāra</s> (poetic figure), like a necklace and the like,
Is a captivating arrangement.
Of masses of vowels and consonants,
Fulfilling the longing of their abundant arrays,
Speech, overflowing with the pride of the world's awakening,
Is resplendent with <s>chekānuprāsa</s> (clever alliteration).
Full of repeated letters,
Speech possessing <s>vṛttyanuprāsa</s> (alliteration of repetition)
[Is] the abode of the freely flowing
Abundance of copious bliss.
The ground of <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> (Lāṭa-alliteration) is repetition
With different intention.
[Example:] Where the roaring of the enemy shall be no more —
That conquered one is [truly] conquered.
If the repetition of letters in a half-verse
Or a quarter-verse is fixed,
Then the wise and good consider it
<s>Sphuṭānuprāsa</s> (clear alliteration).
In the subject of comparison, the standard of comparison, and so on,
<s>Arthānuprāsa</s> (semantic alliteration) is accepted.
[Example:] Sandalwood [paste] indeed is the salutation
To the pair of feet of <s>Govinda</s>.
[There is] <s>punaruktapratīkāśa</s> (resembling verbal repetition)
And <s>punaruktārthasannibha</s> (resembling semantic repetition).
[Example:] Making the edge of [her] garment (<s>aṃśuka</s>) [its] end, the moon
Reaches the end of the sky (<s>ambara</s>).
A cluster of repeated letters,
The sprout and root-bulb of the poet's praise —
The wise know <s>yamaka</s> (paronomasia) as the foremost,
The sweetness-bearer of speech.
<s>Citra</s> (pictorial poetry) — such as sword-diagrams and the like —
Is recognized by the foremost poetry connoisseurs.
Among those, the first is said [to be] a pair of verses
That delights the good.
The sword-line would be like a beautiful woman —
A graceful-handed enchantress,
Anointed with saffron, with reddened body,
Resting near the enemy's throat.
<s>Upamā</s> (simile) is where the splendor of resemblance
Between two things shines forth —
As the breasts of a slender-limbed woman
Sport prominently upon [her] chest.
Where one and the same thing is awake to
[Both] being the standard and the subject of comparison —
As in 'The moon is like the moon' and so on —
That is <s>ananvaya</s> (non-sequential comparison).
If that [mutual comparison] occurs alternately for two [things],
It is considered <s>upameyopamā</s> (mutual simile).
[Example:] <s>Dharma</s> in you is like <s>artha</s>, full of splendor;
<s>Artha</s> [in you] is like <s>dharma</s>.
Where a well-known standard of comparison
Becomes the subject of comparison —
As in 'The moon is like [her] face' and so on —
Then it is <s>pratīpopamā</s> (reversed simile).
When the standard of comparison is enriched with words
Like 'play' (<s>līlā</s>) and the like, it is <s>lalitopamā</s> (graceful simile).
[Example:] Your pair of eyes bears
The playfulness of blue lotuses.
The resemblance of multiple pairs of meanings
Is <s>stabakopamā</s> (cluster-simile).
[Example:] I have taken refuge at the feet of <s>Viṣṇu</s>,
As a bee [takes refuge] in a lotus.
<s>Saṃpūrṇopamā</s> (complete simile) is where
Both [standard and subject] serve as predicates.
[Example:] Like lotuses, wide awake,
Were the eyes at the face of day.
Where the wall made of the subject of comparison
Is entirely painted over with
The picture of the standard of comparison —
There <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) is accepted.
When the superimposition is accomplished through a shared attribute,
It is <s>sopādhirūpaka</s> (conditional metaphor).
[Example:] He is <s>Purandara</s> (Indra) in clipping the wings
Of the target-mountains of arrogant kings.
When the resemblance is stated separately
And visibly, it is <s>sādṛśyarūpaka</s> (resemblance-metaphor).
[Example:] With five radiant branches,
Your arm-tree shines.
Expressions like 'body-staff' (<s>aṅgayaṣṭi</s>) and such
Constitute <s>ābhāsarūpaka</s> (semblance-metaphor).
'Body-staff,' 'bow,' 'creeper,' and the like —
These constitute <s>rūpitarūpaka</s> (fashioned metaphor).
<s>Pariṇāma</s> (transformation) is where the non-difference
Between the two culminates [in actual identity].
[Example:] Asked by her beloved in private,
She gave silence itself as her answer.
The varied description of a single [thing] by many [persons]
Is considered <s>ullekhitā</s> (delineation).
[Example:] He was seen as <s>Kāma</s> by women, as the moon by friends,
As Death by enemies.
<s>Apahnutiḥ</s> (concealment) is the denial of what is real
In order to superimpose what is unreal.
[Example:] This is not the moon — what then?
[It is] a lotus of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>.
<s>Paryastāpahnuti</s> (inverted concealment) is where
Only the attribute is denied.
[Example:] This is not the nectar-rayed one (<s>sudhāṃśu</s>) — what then?
The nectar-rayed one [is] my beloved's face.
<s>Bhrāntāpahnuti</s> (deluded concealment) is when there is doubt
About another [thing] when ascertaining the real one.
[Example:] It produces heat with trembling —
A fever? No, friend, [it is] Love (<s>Smara</s>).
<s>Chekāpahnuti</s> (clever concealment) is the denial
Of the real through suspicion of another [thing].
[Example:] Chattering and clinging to my foot —
My lover? No indeed, [it is merely] an anklet.
<s>Kaitavāpahnuti</s> (deceitful concealment) is concealment
Of something manifest through words like 'pretense' and the like.
[Example:] The arrows of <s>Smara</s> (Love) issue forth
From the pretense of the beloved's glances.
<s>Utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) is where a cause and the like
Is imagined without concealment.
[Example:] Surely on account of the beauty of your face,
The moon harbors enmity toward lotuses.
In the absence of words like 'as if' (<s>iva</s>) and the like,
They call it <s>gūḍhotprekṣā</s> (hidden fancy).
[Example:] Whose fame, weary from wandering,
Entered the celestial river.
Through remembrance (<s>smṛti</s>), delusion (<s>bhrānti</s>), and doubt (<s>saṃdeha</s>) —
Those themselves are a triad of figures.
[Example of <s>smṛti</s>:] Seeing a lotus,
Her face plunges into my mind.
[Example of <s>bhrānti</s>:] This intoxicated bee
Knows your face as a lotus.
[Example of <s>saṃdeha</s>:] Whether it is a lotus or the moon —
For us there is no certainty.
<s>Mīlita</s> (the veiled) is when, due to great resemblance,
Even difference is not perceived.
[Example:] The lac-dye was not perceived
On [her] naturally reddened foot.
<s>Sāmānya</s> (generality) is when, due to resemblance,
Even the distinction itself is not perceived.
[Example:] The faces of the fair-browed women who entered
The lotus-pond were not discerned.
<s>Unmīlita</s> (the revealed) is considered to be the manifestation
[Of something previously veiled] due to some special cause.
[Example:] When the moon rose,
Both lotuses and faces were discerned.
<s>Anumāna</s> (inference) is the ascertainment of the cause and the like
From the effect and the like.
[Example:] There is something [between us], since she,
Looking at me, smiled slightly.
<s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is when a statement about one thing
Establishes another by itself.
[Example:] The moon has been conquered by your face —
What need to speak of lotuses?
<s>Kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic reason) is a verbal meaning
That supports a novel meaning.
[Example:] You are defeated, O dull <s>Kandarpa</s> (Love) —
The three-eyed one (<s>Trilocana</s>) resides in my heart.
<s>Parikara</s> (retinue) is the figure
When a qualifier has an underlying intention.
[Example:] May <s>Śiva</s>, who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
Remove your affliction.
When the qualified [noun] itself has an intention,
It becomes <s>parikarāṅkura</s> (sprout of retinue).
[Example:] The four-armed god (<s>Caturbhuja</s>)
Is the giver of the four <s>puruṣārthas</s> (human goals).
<s>Akramātiśayokti</s> (simultaneous hyperbole) is when
Cause and effect are [represented as] simultaneous.
[Example:] O Lord, simultaneously your arrows

children.text: jyāṃ śarāś ca parāś ca te
children.translated_text: And your enemies embrace the bowstring.
<s>Atyantātiśayokti</s> (extreme hyperbole) is
The transposition of the sequence.
[Example:] First her pride departed; afterward
She was conciliated by her beloved.
<s>Capalātiśayokti</s> (fleeting hyperbole) is
When the effect arises upon the mere occasion of the cause.
[Example:] When the beloved asked 'Shall I go?'
Her bangles became rings.
<s>Sambandhātiśayokti</s> (relational hyperbole) is
A statement asserting [connection] even in its absence.
[Example:] See — the disc of the moon
Shines attached to the top of the palace.
<s>Bhedakātiśayokti</s> (differentiating hyperbole) is when
[Something] is spoken of as another though it is one and the same.
[Example:] Ah, the play of charm
At the young girl's bosom is something else entirely!
<s>Rūpakātiśayokti</s> (metaphorical hyperbole) is when
What is superimposed occurs within a metaphor.
[Example:] See — from the pair of blue lotuses
Issue sharp arrows.
<s>Prauḍhokti</s> (bold utterance) is the supposition
Of capacity in what is incapable.
[Example:] The trees on the bank of the <s>Yamunā</s> (Kalindajā) —
The dark <s>sarala</s> pines [stand] straight.
<s>Sambhāvana</s> (supposition) is the conjecture 'If it were thus'
For the purpose of establishing something else.
[Example:] [The plant is] watered with waters whitened
By being stored inside crystal vessels —
If a pearl-vine were to produce [flowers],
Your fame would equal its blossoms.
<s>Praharṣaṇa</s> (delight) is the effortless attainment
Of more than what was desired.
[Example:] While [one would] light a lamp,
The sun has already risen.
<s>Viṣādana</s> (distress) is the attainment
Of an outcome contrary to what is desired.
[Example:] While [one would] light the lamp,
It is already extinguished.
<s>Tulyayogitā</s> (equal connection) is the equality
Of many [things] through action and the like.
[Example:] Lotuses close up
And the faces of wanton women too,
When the moon, whose disc kisses the peak
Of the eastern mountain, [appears].
<s>Dīpaka</s> (illuminator) is accepted when there is equality
Between the relevant and the irrelevant [subjects].
[Example:] The learned man bears intellect, the moon bears nectar,
And you bear the earth.
When the illuminating word is repeated,
It becomes <s>āvṛttidīpaka</s> (repeated illuminator).
[Example:] Fire shines with glow, the moon shines —
The sun shines with brilliance.
<s>Prativastūpamā</s> (object-for-object simile) is accepted
When there is similarity of meaning between two sentences.
[Example:] The sun blazes with heat;
The hero shines with his bow.
If there is an original-reflection (<s>bimba-pratibimba</s>) relationship,
<s>Dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration) is that figure.
[Example:] In the contest of wrestler against counter-wrestler,
There arises a thunderous war-cry of battle.
[Another <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>:] If your form [is the illustration],
Then that ill-writing of fate is erased.
If the sun's radiance has arisen first,
Then certainly the night has departed.
<s>Nidarśanā</s> (exemplification) is the superimposition of identity
Upon two similar sentence-meanings.
[Example:] The gentleness that belongs to the giver —
That very [thing] is the spotlessness of the moon.
<s>Vyatireka</s> (contrast) is when there is a distinction
Between the standard and the subject of comparison.
[Example:] The good are lofty like mountains,
But [unlike them] are soft by nature.
<s>Sahokti</s> (co-expression) is when there is co-existence.
[Example:] He who delights the people shines —
Whose fame reached the ends of the quarters
Along with his adversaries.
<s>Vinokti</s> (without-expression) is when the relevant [subject]
Is said to be deficient without something.
[Example:] Learning, though pleasing, is flawed
Without the wealth of humility.
<s>Samāsokti</s> (condensed expression) is when the irrelevant [subject]
Becomes manifest within the relevant.
[Example:] See — this reddened moon
Kisses the face of the east (<s>Aindrī</s>).
<s>Khaṇḍaśleṣa</s> (partial paronomasia) is when individual words
Each have separate meanings.
[Example:] Overflowing with copious water [or blood],
The lord of rivers [or lord of armies] shone.
<s>Bhaṅgaśleṣa</s> (split paronomasia) is when the group of words
Itself [taken as a whole] has separate meanings.
[Example:] Whose is the state of being undecaying and immortal (<s>ajarāmaratā</s>)?
Whose city is dear if not <s>Ayodhyā</s> itself?
<s>Arthaśleṣa</s> (semantic paronomasia) is when the meaning alone
Has multiple significations.
[Example:] Crooked, dark, long —
[These describe] both your sidelong glances and your tresses.
<s>Aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant) is that [figure]
Where [the irrelevant] follows the relevant,
Through cause-effect, generality-particularity,
And the like — so it is accepted.
[Example:] What is not made beautiful by lotuses
That are the abode of <s>Kamalā</s> (<s>Lakṣmī</s>)?
Even the far shore of the ocean
Is reached by the industrious.
<s>Arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration) is the statement
Of a connected different meaning.
[Example:] <s>Hanūmān</s> crossed the ocean —
What is difficult for great souls?
<s>Vikasvara</s> (the expansive) is [the figure] in which [there are]
Particulars, a generality, and [again] particulars.
[Example:] He was not conquered — for the great are indeed
Unassailable, like mountains.
When the relevant [subject] is expressed through
Its effects and the like, they call it <s>paryāyokti</s> (periphrasis).
[Example:] Grass sprouted
In the palaces of rival kings.
<s>Vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise) is the expression of praise or blame
Through the [apparent form of] blame or praise respectively.
[Example:] What discrimination is yours, [O king],
That you lead even sinners to heaven!
<s>Ākṣepa</s> (retraction) is the negation of something stated,
Upon reflection.
[Example:] O moon, show yourself!
Or rather — there is [already] my beloved's face.
<s>Gūḍhākṣepa</s> (hidden retraction) is when the injunction is manifest
But the prohibition is not explicit.
[Example:] Carry off <s>Sītā</s> happily — but do consider
The approach of the Destroyer (<s>Antaka</s>).
<s>Virodha</s> (contradiction) is incongruity
In attributes, substances, actions, and the like.
[Example:] The profuse flow of sandalwood [paste]
Freely burns me.
<s>Virodhābhāsa</s> (semblance of contradiction) is accepted when
The contradiction is grounded in paronomasia (<s>śleṣa</s>) and the like.
[Example:] Even by this darkness-maker (<s>Andhakārin</s> [= slayer of Andhaka, i.e. <s>Śiva</s>]),
This world is illuminated.
<s>Asaṃbhava</s> (impossibility) is the description of the inconceivable
In the accomplishment of a meaning.
[Example:] Who knew [that] a cowherd boy
Would uproot a mountain?
<s>Vibhāvanā</s> (causeless effect) is when an effect arises
Even without a cause.
[Example:] See — your pair of feet
Is red [as if] stained with lac-dye.
<s>Viśeṣokti</s> (specialization) is the non-occurrence
Of the effect even when the cause is present.
[Example:] No one transgresses a wise man,
Even when he bows.
<s>Asaṃgati</s> (disconnection) is when cause and effect
Occur in different locations though [seemingly] connected.
[Example:] The bodies of your devotees bow [to you],
[And] the weariness of worldly existence breaks apart.
<s>Viṣama</s> (incongruity) is the combination of many things
That lack fitness with one another.
[Example:] Where [are] the fiercely venomous serpents,
And where [is] that sandalwood tree?
<s>Sama</s> (congruity) is the description of the connection
Of many things based on fitness.
[Example:] A fitting abode has been made —
The bosom-region by the pearl necklace.
<s>Vicitra</s> (the paradoxical) is when effort
Yields an opposite result.
[Example:] The good bow down even before the three worlds
In order to gain elevation.
<s>Adhika</s> (the excessive) is when the thing contained
Is described as exceeding the container.
[Example:] Your qualities do not fit within that speech
By which the world is pervaded.
<s>Anyonya</s> (mutual [relation]) is where there is
Reciprocal benefit.
[Example:] The night shines by the moon;
The moon shines by the night.
<s>Viśeṣa</s> (distinction) is the description of the contained
Without the well-known container.
[Example:] Even when the sun has departed, its rays,
Stationed in lamps, cut through the darkness.
<s>Vyāghāta</s> (reversal) is when an otherwise-acting thing
Is said to perform a different action.
[Example:] The Flower-armed one (<s>Kusumāyudha</s>, i.e. <s>Kāma</s>) slays with those very [flowers]
By which the world is pleased.
<s>Gumpha</s> (chain) would be a garland of causes —
as before, through successive causes—
through statecraft [comes] prosperity, through prosperity [comes] renunciation,
through renunciation, vast fame.
A succession of meanings in the manner of 'taken and released'
is considered <s>ekāvalī</s> (string of pearls).
The eyes resting at the edge of the ears,
the ears swaying at the base of the arms.
The combination of <s>dīpaka</s> (illuminator) and <s>ekāvalī</s> (chain)
is called <s>mālādīpaka</s> (garland-illuminator).
By <s>Smara</s> (Love) in her heart, by her
in you, an abode has been made.
<s>Sāra</s> (essence) is the successive elevation of expressions
in terms of their essentiality.
Among [excellent things], the <s>Sārasvata</s> is essential; among those, poetry;
among those, the hymn to <s>Śiva</s>.
If what is noble-and-essential shines as
a quality distinct [yet] appearing as non-distinct—
sweet is honey, [sweeter] is nectar,
[sweeter] than that, the poet's speech.
<s>Yathāsaṃkhya</s> (numerical correspondence) [obtains when] two groups of meanings
are connected one-by-one in sequence.
The enemy, the friend, the adversary's faction—
conquer, delight, and shatter [respectively].
<s>Paryāya</s> (succession) [obtains when]
one [entity] has connection to many [in sequence].
Having left the lotus, [the comparison for] a beautiful woman's face
has gone to the moon.
<s>Parivṛtti</s> (exchange) is the mutual
interchange of the lesser and the greater.
He seized one arrow, having released
the side-glances of the enemy's women.
<s>Parisaṃkhyā</s> (restriction by enumeration) is, by excluding one,
the constraining [of something] to another locus.
The depletion of oil [occurs] in lamps,
not in the hearts of [women] with arched brows.
<s>Vikalpa</s> (alternative) is the clever opposition
of two equally strong [elements].
In the beloved's heart or in her lip—
establish your detachment!
<s>Samuccaya</s> (accumulation) is the interweaving of many
[elements] sharing one connection.
They perish, afterward they see,
and they fall—your enemies.
<s>Samādhi</s> (coincidence) is the ease of an effect
from the proximity of another cause.
Making her long [for him],
the sun also set.
<s>Pratyanīka</s> (adversarial) is valor
on the side of a powerful enemy.
The ears, following the conquering eyes,
are humbled by the [blue] lotuses.
<s>Pratīpa</s> (reverse simile) is the inferiority
of the standard of comparison relative to the object compared.
If her face has been seen,
what [use] is a lotus? What [use] the moon?
<s>Ullāsa</s> (exultation) [obtains when] through another's greatness,
a fault is described elsewhere.
That is merely the misfortune of wealth itself,
that it does not resort to good people.
<s>Tadguṇa</s> (acquiring another's quality) is the arising of a [new] quality from another,
with the abandonment of one's own quality.
The pearl on your nose, resting on your lip,
has become ruby-red.
The re-attainment of one's own quality
is to be known as <s>pūrvarūpatā</s> (reversion to former state).
Even though smeared by the rays from <s>Hara</s>'s throat,
<s>Śeṣa</s> is white by your fame.
When an object's form [becomes] otherwise
and then [reverts]—that too is <s>pūrvarūpatā</s>.
When the lamp was extinguished, there was
day-splendor from the gems of the girdle.
When, despite contact with another's quality, one does not take on
that quality—this they call <s>atadguṇa</s> (non-acquisition).
Even though entering the middle of the sun,
the moon is always cool.
The heightening of one's own previously established quality
from the proximity of another is <s>anuguṇa</s> (conforming quality).
The ear-lotuses acquire
even more blueness from the side-glances.
<s>Avajñā</s> (contempt) is described when an object
is presented as incapable of merit or demerit.
If the lotuses wilt,
what loss is it to the moon?
<s>Praśnottara</s> (question-and-answer) [obtains when] answers
are woven together sequentially in the discourse.
'Where is that willow, O traveler?'
'There is the easily-crossable river.'
<s>Pihita</s> (concealment) is the action, by one who knows
another's secret, to conceal [it] from another.
When the beloved came home in the morning,
the wife [hurriedly] made the bed.
<s>Vyājoktī</s> (pretextual speech) is the concealment of a matter by pretense,
by one who is apprehensive.
'Friend, look—by the pollen of the garden
I have become dusted gray!'
<s>Vakroktī</s> (oblique speech) is the fabrication of a different expressed meaning
through paronomasia (<s>śleṣa</s>) or shift of tone (<s>kāku</s>).
'Release your pride! The day has come!'
'Slowly—<s>Nandī</s> is near <s>Hara</s>!'
<s>Svābhāvoktī</s> (natural description) is the description of the nature
[of things] such as class and the rest.
[She] is gazed at by deer with wavering eyes
and motionless ears.
<s>Bhāvika</s> (visionary description) is the description as if directly seeing
a past or future event.
Behold! Even today
the gods and demons fight here.
<s>Bhāvikacchavī</s> (visionary coloring) is the depiction of something
spatially or temporally distant [as if seen].
You, dwelling in her heart,
are seen directly as the five-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>).
<s>Udātta</s> (noble description) is the praiseworthy conduct of great ones
serving as an indirect characterization of another.
On whose peak the battle took place—
that of <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) and <s>Kirīṭin</s> (<s>Arjuna</s>).
<s>Atyuktī</s> (hyperbole) is the description of wondrous, incredible
valor, magnanimity, and the like.
When you are the giver, O lord of kings,
the beggars are [like] wish-fulfilling trees.
Based on <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, their semblances,
and the tranquility of <s>bhāva</s>—
[the ornaments are named] <s>rasavat</s>, <s>preyas</s>, <s>ūrjasvī</s>,
<s>samāhita</s>, and those based on semblances.
The arising of emotions, their junction,
and their intermixture—thus three [more].
Some wise [scholars] declare
these seven ornaments.
Purity (<s>śuddhi</s>) is the predominance of one;
and [also there are] <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (blending) and <s>saṃkara</s> (mixing).
These are [merely] arrangements of these same [alaṅkāras],
not separate ornaments.
For all [alaṅkāras] bearing the designation
of rival or imitation—
the distinguishing condition, though manifest somewhere,
would also be possible elsewhere.
<s>Mālā</s> (garland) and <s>paramparā</s> (succession) [occur]
when many of these are favorable [to each other].
In a human composition, somewhere
[an alaṅkāra may] attain the status of a subordinate element.
In word, in meaning, in sentence-meaning,
and in a cluster of sentence-meanings—
these [alaṅkāras] occur as arrangements
of natural and heightened [types].
Since the expression of any heightened [quality] whatsoever—
by this analysis of the true meaning—
for the most part these ornaments
are not distinct from <s>atiśayoktī</s> (hyperbole).
Among those [ornaments] that are alaṅkāra-predominant,
even when bearing similarity—
individuality [shines] distinctly in each instance,
as in faces.
If the learned have no regard
for the established [classification of] ornaments,
then let the catalogue of names
be desired [at least] for the newer varieties.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in sacrificial learning headed by the <s>satra</s>,
and <s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind is directed by devotion to him—these are his parents.
This is the fourth [chapter], together with one [more], in the <s>Candrāloka</s> composed by the good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>—
may [this] ray long delight the minds of the good.
The cause (<s>vibhāva</s>), consisting of the foundational (<s>ālambana</s>) and stimulating (<s>uddīpana</s>) [types],
is twofold.
The effect is the <s>anubhāva</s> (consequent); and the accompanying
emotion (<s>bhāva</s>) is also the transitory (<s>vyabhicārin</s>).
Bursting forth, dissolving the distinction between
subject and object, in the hearts of those of sensitive nature,
like the contact of sandalwood paste
blooming delight—
in poetry, drama, and [their] effects,
manifested by <s>vibhāvas</s> and the rest,
savored as a unified experience,
the permanent emotion (<s>sthāyibhāva</s>) is known as <s>rasa</s>.
Having the permanent emotion called <s>rati</s> (love) as its essence,
manifested by <s>vibhāvas</s> such as the beloved and the like,
accompanied by <s>vyabhicārins</s> except for laziness, envy,
and disgust—
with <s>anubhāvas</s> such as side-glances and the like,
[and <s>vyabhicārins</s> such as] delirium and the like, respectively,
<s>sambhoga</s> (union) and <s>vipralambha</s> (separation)—
<s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) is considered to be of two kinds.
The permanent emotion of laughter—<s>hāsya-rasa</s> (comic sentiment)
[is manifested] by <s>vibhāvas</s> and the rest, respectively,
[such as] deformity, puffed cheeks,
dissimulation and the like—accompanied [by these].
Separation from the beloved, tears,
falling, languor, and the rest—by these, respectively,
the <s>vibhāvas</s> and the rest being present, with grief (<s>śoka</s>)
as the permanent emotion—that is <s>karuṇa-rasa</s> (pathetic sentiment).
With anger (<s>krodha</s>) as the permanent emotion, <s>raudra-rasa</s> (furious sentiment)
is accompanied by <s>vibhāvas</s> and the rest—
jealousy, striking with the hand,
delusion, and the like, respectively.
The permanent emotion called <s>utsāha</s> (enthusiasm),
arising from <s>vibhāvas</s> such as power and the like—
<s>vīra-rasa</s> (heroic sentiment), with <s>anubhāvas</s> such as steadfastness and the like,
accompanied by <s>bhāvas</s> such as pride and the rest.
With <s>vibhāvas</s> such as tigers and the like,
bearing <s>anubhāvas</s> such as trembling and the rest,
accompanied by <s>bhāvas</s> such as delusion and the like,
with fear (<s>bhaya</s>) as permanent emotion—<s>bhayānaka</s> (fearful sentiment).
With disgust (<s>jugupsā</s>) as the permanent emotion, <s>bībhatsa</s> (repulsive sentiment)—
the <s>vibhāvas</s> and the rest, respectively,
are seeing the unpleasant, spitting,
delusion and the like—where these are established.
<s>Adbhuta</s> (wondrous sentiment), with wonder (<s>vismaya</s>) as permanent emotion,
arising from <s>vibhāvas</s> such as magic and the like,
this [rasa] has <s>anubhāvas</s> such as horripilation and the rest,
with <s>vyabhicārins</s> such as stupefaction and the like.
<s>Śānta</s> (tranquil sentiment), with dispassion (<s>nirveda</s>) as permanent emotion,
arising from <s>vibhāvas</s> such as the company of the good and the like,
this [rasa] has <s>anubhāvas</s> such as patience and the rest,
with <s>vyabhicārins</s> such as stupefaction and the like.
<s>Rati</s> (love), when directed toward gods and the like,
and the <s>vyabhicārins</s> (transitory emotions)—
those that are known [as such] are called
<s>bhāvas</s> (emotions) by the knowers of literary science.
Dispassion (<s>nirveda</s>), languor (<s>glāni</s>), apprehension (<s>śaṅkā</s>),
envy (<s>asūyā</s>), intoxication (<s>mada</s>), weariness (<s>śrama</s>),
laziness (<s>ālasya</s>), and dejection (<s>dainya</s>),
anxiety (<s>cintā</s>), delusion (<s>moha</s>), recollection (<s>smṛti</s>), resolve (<s>dhṛti</s>),
bashfulness (<s>vrīḍā</s>), fickleness (<s>capalatā</s>), joy (<s>harṣa</s>),
agitation (<s>āvega</s>), stupor (<s>jaḍatā</s>),
pride (<s>garva</s>), despair (<s>viṣāda</s>), longing (<s>autsukyam</s>),
drowsiness (<s>nidrā</s>), and catalepsy (<s>apasmāra</s>),
dreaming (<s>supta</s>), awakening (<s>prabodha</s>), indignation (<s>amarṣa</s>),
dissimulation (<s>avahittha</s>), and ferocity (<s>ugratā</s>),
reflection (<s>mati</s>), sickness (<s>vyādhi</s>), and madness (<s>unmāda</s>),
and death (<s>maraṇa</s>) as well,
fright (<s>trāsa</s>) and doubt (<s>vitarka</s>)—
these are to be known as the <s>vyabhicārins</s> (transitory emotions).
These thirty-three <s>bhāvas</s>
have been enumerated by name.
Through universal, non-specific love,
and through humility and the rest as their nature,
through impropriety—<s>rasābhāsas</s> (semblances of rasa)
and <s>bhāvābhāsas</s> (semblances of emotion) are declared.
The tranquility of emotion, its arising,
its junction, and its intermixture—
for poetry, like saffron
for gold, [they serve as] an enhancement of luster.
Urgency [requires] up to seven [compounds];
with chosen [words], from the eighth onward,
there should be compounding; with [words] there should not be
compounding in every case.
<s>Pāñcālī</s> and <s>Lāṭīyā</s>,
<s>Gauḍīyā</s> and, following the respective <s>rasas</s>,
<s>Vaidarbhī</s>—in numerical order,
four <s>rītis</s> (literary styles) are recognized.
In the sweet [style], the consonants are dominated by
the class-fifth nasals of their own groups,
the letter <s>la</s> and <s>la</s> conjoined,
with short and separated <s>ra</s> and <s>ṇa</s>.
Dominated by <s>repha</s>, the class-consonants and <s>ya</s>, <s>ṇa</s>,
except for the <s>ṭa</s>-class and the fifth [nasal],
the <s>ta</s>-class dominated by <s>ka</s> and <s>pa</s>—
and in the vigorous [style], <s>ka</s> and <s>ma</s> at the head.
With all upper [consonants] conjoined with <s>sa</s>,
with all [consonants] conjoined with <s>repha</s> throughout,
a twofold conjunction of <s>ra</s> and <s>ha</s>—
in the harsh [style], <s>śa</s> and <s>ṣa</s> by themselves.
The letter <s>la</s> unconjoined with others,
light [syllables], <s>gha</s>, <s>bha</s>, <s>dha</s>, and soft <s>ra</s>-sounds—
in the graceful [style]; and the rest
in the gentle [style]—thus are the <s>vṛttis</s> (modes).
A young woman, radiant with the play of swaying limbs,
a triumphal arch of love—
for those of keen intellect, full of hard reasoning,
[such description] is in vain.
Eager, uplifted-faced, with moist lips—
the peacock drank, lean, the thirst;
the woman impetuously embraces
when the cloud-canopy swells.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in sacrificial learning headed by the <s>satra</s>,
and <s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind is directed by devotion to him—these are his parents.
May this ray, by that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed
<s>Candrāloka</s>, long delight the great [audience], numbered as the seasons.
Endowed with three varieties of <s>vṛtti</s> (mode),
like the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (Ganges) with [her] streams,
<s>Bhāratī</s> (speech) shines forth, profound,
crooked [here], straight elsewhere.
Of speech that is openly directed
toward another meaning—
like the sidelong glance of a woman with restless eyes,
the function is of the nature of suggestion (<s>vyañjanā</s>).
Of [<s>dhvani</s> whose literal meaning is] not intended (<s>avivakṣita-vācya</s>),
there are two varieties: the expressed meaning is either
transferred to another meaning (<s>arthāntara-saṅkramita</s>)
or completely concealed (<s>atyanta-tiraskṛta</s>).
Of [<s>dhvani</s> whose literal meaning is] intended (<s>vivakṣita-vācya</s>),
there are two [sub-types]: with perceptible and imperceptible sequence.
With the addition of forty-one,
the [total] varieties of these two are six in sequence.
Threefold—born from the power of word, meaning, and their combination—
[is the type] of perceptible sequence;
headed by <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, their semblances—
[is the type] of imperceptible sequence.
Of the manifestation of content (<s>vastu</s>) and ornament (<s>alaṅkāra</s>),
two varieties are born from word-power;
of that which arises from meaning-power,
there are twelve varieties—thus:
four [types]: content [manifesting] ornament,
ornament [manifesting] content,
ornament [manifesting] ornament,
and content [manifesting] content.
The suggestive meaning—composed by the speaker,
skillfully created by the poet,
self-arisen, or of a different nature—
four [types], threefold [by quality]—thus,
based on word, meaning, or both—one [type]
resting on a single sentence;
in a part of a word, in composition,
in phonemes, in sentence, and in word—
and in a literary composition—thus sixfold,
called <s>rasa</s> and the rest, of imperceptible sequence.
Among these seventeen, setting aside one—
the imperceptible-sequence [type]—
the first sixteen, doubled,
become [thirty-two] through sentence and word bases.
In composition too, twelve arise
as varieties born from meaning-power.
Thirty-two, twelve, one, and six—
the total varieties of <s>dhvani</s>
are fifty-one;
and the mixed [varieties] are thousands.
Composed by the speaker—to convey
the suggested meaning desired by the speaker;
self-arisen—of a different nature,
spontaneously blooming from speech itself.
Some [hearer] is common; some
is made to understand by being addressed;
some is a bystander; and some
is one who understands what is [already] understood.
Thus, from the variety of comprehenders,
the speaker-composed [type] is fourfold.
Through neglect (<s>upekṣā</s>) and concealment (<s>nihnava</s>),
the self-arisen [type] is considered twofold.
Through the distinction of tenses—past and the rest—
concealment (<s>nihnava</s>) is of many kinds.
By this variety also,
the vine of manifestation (<s>vyakti</s>) flourishes.
The manifold varieties, determined
by context and the like in some [cases]—
when a meaning expresses another meaning—
that is accepted as <s>vācya-vyaṅgya</s> (expressed-suggested).
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in sacrificial learning headed by the <s>satra</s>,
and <s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind is directed by devotion to him—these are his parents.
<s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray) -- by that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed
<s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight), may he long delight, [this is chapter] numbered seven (muni-number).
That which, when suggested, brings about
stillness of the mind -- that is <s>dhvani</s> (resonance). Otherwise, however, <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion)
is regarded as threefold
in its occurrence.
Sometimes the manifestation itself is the suggested sense,
sometimes due to the inherent nature of the meaning,
and sometimes before something more charming,
it relinquishes its own charm.
The unconcealed type should be understood as involving transference to another meaning and so forth --
[Example:]
'O lord of the waters, have you forgotten
that <s>Kumbhasambhava</s> (jar-born <s>Agastya</s>)?'
When another <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) etc. becomes
subordinate to a [dominant] <s>rasa</s> etc. -- [Example:]
'Alas! My breast, smeared with saffron from my bosom,
has been pierced by arrows!'
Likewise, when an auxiliary element serves the accomplishment of the literal meaning,
as a boat serves the purpose of [crossing] the ocean -- [Example:]
'The steadfast, having resorted to a boat,
cross the oceans of disease.'
The indistinct type: here, the resemblance of the breasts
to <s>cakravāka</s> birds is considered [merely implied] -- [Example:]
'The pair of breasts anointed with saffron
plunges into my <s>Mānasa</s> lake (mind).'
The doubtful type: when there is uncertainty
regarding length etc., as with blue lotuses -- [Example:]
'When her eyes have reached
the position of ear-ornaments,'
the equal-prominence type: bearing similarity with the literal meaning
like moonhood -- [Example:]
'O beloved, by the radiance of your face,
the lotus languishes.'
The unbeautiful type: when the suggested sense
is less charming than the literal meaning -- [Example:]
'On the lake where lotuses have closed,
the <s>cakravāka</s> bird gazes at his beloved.'
'The ocean bowed to <s>Kākutstha</s> (<s>Rāma</s>);
let <s>Rāvaṇa</s> now revel!' --
Thus, <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion) has been recognized
by the learned as eightfold.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in the lore of sacrifices led by <s>Satra</s>,
<s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted through devotion to him -- these two were his parents.
<s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray) -- by that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed
<s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight), may [this chapter] numbered eight (vasu-number) long delight.
When the primary meaning is not intended,
conventional in earlier and later usage,
and connected with a purpose --
that which speaks [thus] is recognized as <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification).
By the inclusion or exclusion of the word's own [primary] meaning
that is to be indicated, <s>lakṣaṇā</s> is twofold.
That [lakṣaṇā] is [further] threefold by the distinction of <s>siddha</s> (established),
<s>sādhya</s> (to-be-accomplished), and <s>sādhyāṅga</s> (subsidiary-to-be-accomplished).
By the distinction of manifest and non-manifest,
the purpose also is twofold.
The learned know the manifest [purpose] as twofold:
due to being extrinsic and due to being intrinsic to the meaning.
The non-manifest [purpose] also is twofold: due to being intrinsic to the meaning
and due to being extrinsic.
That which is intrinsic to the meaning is also twofold,
due to residing in the indicated or in the indicator.
Where the manifest [purpose] resides in the indicator,
that is called <s>vicakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇā</s> (perspicuous secondary signification).
The non-manifest, the extrinsic,
and that residing in the indicated --
these are the other three. Thus, by [verbal] power, it is fourfold.
[Example of vicakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇā:]
'This moon itself is her face' --
excellence is indicated in the face.
[Example:] In 'increase the lamp' --
the extrinsic [purpose] is the arising of auspiciousness.
[Example:] In 'this cloth is burnt' and so forth,
the manifest purpose does not exist [i.e., no aesthetic purpose].
[Example:] In 'the good saying is nectar' and so forth,
[the purpose] resides in the indicated -- extreme delightfulness.
<s>Lakṣaṇā</s> operates due to proximity, contiguity,
apprehension of similar form,
cause-effect relation,
relation of signified and signifier,
and from such connections and so forth.
Also from another set of four:
from similarity, from inherence,
from contrariety, and from connection with action.
The two types called <s>sāropa</s> (superimposition) and <s>adhyavasāna</s> (identification)
are each divided into <s>gauṇa</s> (figurative) and <s>śuddha</s> (pure).
The figurative <s>sāropa</s> type is illustrated
by [the expression] 'the moon is [her] face.'
The figurative <s>adhyavasāna</s> type would be
[the expression] 'this is the moon itself.'
The pure <s>sāropa</s> type is illustrated
by [the expression] 'ghee is life.'
The pure <s>adhyavasāna</s> type would be
[the expression] 'this is life itself.'
Through the modes of <s>upādāna</s> (taking up) and <s>arpaṇa</s> (attribution),
there are two more, thus making six types.
[Example of upādāna:] 'The spears enter the <s>Gaṅgā</s>' [meaning: the villages on the Ganges],
and [example of arpaṇa:] 'the hamlet dwells' [meaning: the people of the hamlet dwell].
Due to the distinctive features of the indicated and the indicator
[respectively], it is again twofold.
[Example:] 'Charming poetry is nectar;
learning is the most enduring wealth.'
Also in some cases, it is divided by the distinction
of having a reason and not having a reason.
[Example:] 'He, by his beauty, is <s>Kandarpa</s> (the god of love),
and she is <s>Rati</s> (love) incarnate.'
In the word, in the meaning of a word, in the meaning of a sentence,
in number, in grammatical case,
and in gender -- this [lakṣaṇā] exists
as the seed-sprout of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (poetic ornamentation).
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in the lore of sacrifices led by <s>Satra</s>,
<s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted through devotion to him -- these two were his parents.
<s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray) -- by that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed
<s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight), may [this chapter] numbered nine (nava-number) long delight.
A word generally operates
by presupposing some property.
That [function] by which a word clearly expresses a meaning
is known by the learned as <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation).
Through <s>jāti</s> (generic property), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), <s>kriyā</s> (action),
<s>vastuyoga</s> (association with a thing), <s>saṃjñā</s> (proper name),
and <s>nirdeśa</s> (designation) -- thus the learned
declare <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation) to be sixfold.
'Cow,' 'blue,' 'cook,' 'staff-bearer,'
'<s>Ḍittha</s>,' '<s>Kaṃsa</s>' -- respectively [are examples of the six types].
[Etymology:] '<s>Kaṃsa</s>' -- he who destroys happiness; the enemy of <s>Kaṃsa</s> [is <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>],
and also 'a man who has resorted to happiness.'
This designation-word is not based on
compounding etc., nor is it a house of convention;
it operates through its primary [function],
its own denotative power.
Born from a shower of nectar,
the <s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight) is enchanting.
Having reached this treasury of ambrosia,
O wise ones, embrace delight!
Victorious are the words of the poet <s>Jayadeva</s>,
born from the body of the illustrious sacrificer <s>Mahādeva</s>,
[words that are] a shower of the nectar
of good sayings.
<s>Mahādeva</s>, solely skilled in the lore of sacrifices led by <s>Satra</s>,
<s>Sumitrā</s>, whose mind was devoted through devotion to him -- these two were his parents.
<s>Mayūkha</s> (Ray) -- by that good poet <s>Jayadeva</s>, in the composed
<s>Candrāloka</s> (Moonlight), may [this chapter] numbered ten (daśa-number) long delight.
